newsitem.title: UK: PRESS DIGEST - Financial Times - March 3.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - Financial Times - March 3.

text.p: Prepared for Reuters by The Broadcast Monitoring Company
-- INSURERS IN PENSION PAY-OUT TALKS

Top insurance executives are considering plans to guarantee retirement benefits to up to 500,000 victims of improperly sold personal pensions. Under the proposals, victims would be guaranteed the same final pay-out from their personal pension as they would have received from the occupational scheme they left. The long-running wrangle over mis-sold pensions is likely to cost the industry up to 4 billion stg in compensation and costs.
-- BANK OF ENGLAND WARNS ON BONUSES

A Bank of England study will warn on Monday that badly structured bonuses may be encouraging traders in the financial markets to take more risks than their employers want. The report in the Bank's Financial Stability Review expresses concern about the one-way nature of the bonuses, whereby traders benefit if they generate profits for the business but suffer no loss themselves should they lose the company money.
-- ORION CREDITORS MAY SOON GET 15 PERCENT OF AGREED CLAIMS

The High Court will this week rule on whether to sanction a plan to begin paying off the debts of insolvent insurance company Orion, years earlier than expected. Thousands of creditors claim they are owed a total of $2 billion (1.2 billion stg) by Orion. Under the proposed scheme, about 15 percent of the agreed claims would be met initially, though this figure could eventually rise to more than 50 percent of the claims.
-- MERRILL LYNCH SET TO PICK CITY FOR HQ

US stockbroker Merrill Lynch is reported to be about to invest more than 200 million stg in a new headquarters building in the City of London. The move would come as a blow to London's Docklands area, which is said to have been considered as an alternative site by Merrill Lynch. A spokesman for the US firm said no decision had been made on the choice of location for the building, but reports suggest it will be at the site of the former Post Office building in King Edward Street, in the City.
-- RURAL WALES FEARS EU AID CUT

The Development Board for Rural Wales has warned that any cuts in European funding will damage the fragile economy of the region. The board is concerned that rural Wales may lose its Objective 5b status, which allows it access to structural funds earmarked for declining rural regions, when the European Commission redraws the map in 1999. Launching a strategy document, David Rowe-Beddoe, chairman of the agency, called for continued recognition of the special needs of rural Wales.
-- SWISS PLAN TELECOMS FLOAT IN FIRST BIG SELL-OFF

The Swiss government plans to sell up to 49 percent of telecoms carrier Swiss Telecom in the country's first big privatisation. The IPO could raise up to SFr5 billion (2.1 billion stg) on the global capital markets. Swiss Telecom has one of the highest density phone networks in the world, and is the seventh biggest market in outgoing telephone calls.
-- RANDGOLD'S EXPLORATION ARM HEADS FOR MARKET

South Africa's Randgold is planning a London stock exchange listing for its international exploration and mining offshoot, Randgold Resources. The IPO, which will be one of the biggest by a gold mining company, will take place before the end of June. Randgold will raise about 100 million stg from the float, which will value Randgold Resources at about 400 million stg.
-- CHIROSCIENCE TO UNVEIL CANCER THERAPY DRUG

Biotechnology company Chiroscience is to hold a briefing for analysts on Monday in which it is expected to announce it has identified a potential cancer therapy that it hopes to put into clinical trials later this year. The new drug is based on Marimastat, the product that has propelled developer British Biotech into the UK's largest biotechnology company. The presentation is also expected to give details of Chiroscience's lead product levobupivacaine, an anaesthetic.
-- ISUZU CLAIMS BETTER DIESEL ENGINE

Japanese vehicle maker Isuzu says it has developed a diesel engine that is twice as fuel-efficient as a comparable petrol engine. The direct-injection engine is also claimed to be 30 percent smaller and 25 percent lighter than other diesel engines. Isuzu plans to use the engines in vehicles made by German's Adam Opel, a subsidiary of General Motors. GM owns 37.4 percent of Isuzu.
-- SHARP FALL IN CHIP PRICES HURTS TOSHIBA

Japanese electronics company Toshiba has issued a warning that profits for the year to March will be lower than expected due to a sharp fall in semiconductor prices, sluggishness in consumer electronics sales and a decline in orders for heavy electrical equipment. Pre-tax profits are likely to be Y120 billion, instead of the Y160 forecast, although the weaker Yen means the results will not be as bad as they could have been.
